'''''Ageratina ligustrina''''', the '''privet-leaved ageratina''' or '''privet-leaved snakeroot''', is [[Mesoamerica]]n [[species]] of [[evergreen]] flowering [[shrub]] in the [[Asteraceae|sunflower family]]. It is widespread across much of [[Mexico]] and [[Central America]] from [[Tamaulipas]] to [[Costa Rica]].<ref>Turner, B. L. 1997. The Comps of Mexico: A systematic account of the family Asteraceae, vol. 1 -- Eupatorieae. Phytologia Memoirs 11: i–iv, 1–272</ref><ref>Linares, J. L. 2003 [2005]. Listado comentado de los árboles nativos y cultivados en la república de El Salvador. Ceiba 44(2): 105–268.</ref><ref>Berendsohn, W.G., A. K. Gruber & J. A. Monterrosa Salomón. 2009. Nova silva cuscatlanica. Árboles nativos e introducidos de El Salvador. Parte 1: Angiospermae - Familias A a L. Englera 29(1): 1–438.</ref>

''Ageratina ligustrina'' grows to 4 metres tall, producing flat heads of daisy-like white to pink [[pseudanthium|composite]] flower-heads in autumn.<ref name=":0">{{cite book|title=RHS A-Z encyclopedia of garden plants|publisher=Dorling Kindersley|year=2008|isbn=978-1405332965|location=United Kingdom|pages=1136}}</ref> The fragrant flower-heads may be up to 20 centimeters in diameter and attract [[Butterfly|butterflies]].<ref>{{Cite web|title=Ageratina ligustrina {{!}} Coastal Hedging|url=https://www.coastalhedging.co.uk/shop/evergreen-hedging-shrubs/ageratina-ligustrina|access-date=2021-04-23|website=www.coastalhedging.co.uk}}</ref> The [[Leaf|leaves]] are light green, elliptic to lance shaped, with toothed margins.<ref name=":1">{{Cite web|last=Shoot|title=Ageratina ligustrina Eupatorium ligustrinum Eupatorium micranthum Eupatorium weinmannianum Privet-leaved eupatorium Care Plant Varieties & Pruning Advice|url=https://www.shootgardening.co.uk/plant/ageratina-ligustrina|access-date=2021-04-23|website=www.shootgardening.co.uk|language=en}}</ref>

== Cultivation ==
''Ageratina ligustrina'' has been in cultivation since the mid 1800s, and in 1996, it gained the [[Royal Horticultural Society]]'s [[Award of Garden Merit]].<ref>{{Cite journal|last=Hind|first=Nicholas|date=2006|title=567. AGERATINA LIGUSTRINA: Compositae|url=https://www.jstor.org/stable/45066102|journal=Curtis's Botanical Magazine|volume=23|issue=4|pages=278–288|issn=1355-4905}}</ref><ref>{{cite web|title=RHS Plant Selector - ''Ageratina ligustrina''|url=http://apps.rhs.org.uk/plantselector/plant?plantid=5592|access-date=19 July 2013}}</ref> It is not fully [[hardiness (plants)|hardy]] in [[temperateness|temperate]] regions.<ref name=":0" /> In the [[United States|US]], it is suitable to be grown outdoors in [[hardiness zone]]s 9–11.<ref name=":1" /> ''A. ligustrina'' tends to be susceptible to [[slug]]s and [[aphid]]s if grown outside, and [[Whitefly|whiteflies]] and [[Tetranychus urticae|red spider mites]] if grown in a greenhouse.<ref>{{Cite web|title=Eupatorium Ligustrinum from Burncoose Nurseries|url=https://www.burncoose.co.uk/site/plants.cfm?pl_id=1835|url-status=live|access-date=April 23, 2021|website=Burncoose Nurseries|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20111014051318/http://www.burncoose.co.uk/site/plants.cfm?pl_id=1835|archive-date=2011-10-14}}</ref>

==Etymology==
''Ageratina'' is derived from [[Greek language|Greek]] meaning 'un-aging', in reference to the flowers keeping their color for a long time. This name was used by [[Dioscorides]] for a number of different plants.<ref name="gledhill">Gledhill, David (2008). "The Names of Plants". Cambridge University Press. {{ISBN|9780521866453}} (hardback), {{ISBN|9780521685535}} (paperback).  pp 39</ref>

The Latin [[Botanical name#Binary name|specific epithet]] ''ligustrina'' highlights the plant's resemblance to the privet ''[[Ligustrum]]'', though the two plants are not believed to be closely related.<ref name=RHSLG>{{cite book|last=Harrison|first=Lorraine|title=RHS Latin for gardeners|year=2012|publisher=Mitchell Beazley|location=United Kingdom|isbn=9781845337315|pages=224}}</ref>

==Chemical compounds==
[[Eupalin]] and [[eupatolin]] are flavonol [[rhamnoside]]s isolated from ''E. ligustrinum''.<ref>The structures of eupalin and eupatolin. Two new flavonol rhamnosides isolated from Eupatorium ligustrinum D.C. L. Quijano, F. Malanco and Tirso Ríos, Tetrahedron, Volume 26, Issue 12, 1970, pages 2851-2859, {{doi|10.1016/S0040-4020(01)92863-7}}</ref>
